title: Scarcity and economising
context: Analyze scarcity, economising, and who participates in economic decision-making. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Scarcity disappears once a household earns a steady salary because income removes all limits.
Economising means making careful use of limited resources rather than treating them as if they were unlimited.
Nobody can fully opt out of economic decisions, because even inaction is a choice about scarce time or money.
Only registered businesses face scarcity; households with regular income never need to economise on their spending.
Exchange requires that at least one party is an entrepreneur; households can never participate directly in exchange.
tactical_explanations:
A salary reallocates scarcity; it does not erase it. Even with steady pay, the household still has a finite budget and finite time — it cannot buy everything at once.

So the statement is False.

Economising is careful use of limited resources. Treating money, time, or materials as if they were infinite is the opposite of that idea.

So the statement is True.

Skipping a purchase is still a decision about scarce time or money. Inaction does not remove you from the set of economic choices; it is one of them. Nobody gets a clean exit simply by doing nothing.

So the statement is True.

Households with regular income still face limited budgets and must choose what to buy. Scarcity is not reserved for registered firms — families economise every week on rent, food, and leisure.

So the statement is False.

Households exchange whenever they buy bread, pay for a haircut, or sell a used bike. Entrepreneur status is not a ticket of admission to trade.

So the statement is False.

title: Goods, services, needs, and wants
context: Analyze the distinction between goods, services, needs, and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Goods must be intangible; any tangible item automatically counts as a service instead.
Services are intangible activities performed for someone, such as installing software or preparing a drink.
Needs are things necessary for well-being, whereas wants are desired but not essential for basic well-being.
Both households and businesses have needs that may be fulfilled through exchange with other economic actors.
Scarcity means resources are limited, so individuals and businesses must economise rather than assume unlimited supply.
tactical_explanations:
Goods are tangible items — a loaf, a phone, a coat. Intangible activities (repairs, lessons, software installs) are services, not goods. The claim swaps the two labels.

So the statement is False.

A service is an intangible activity done for someone: installing software or preparing a drink fits that test.

So the statement is True.

Needs keep basic well-being going; wants are desired extras that are not essential. That split is exactly what the statement reports.

So the statement is True.

Families need food and shelter; firms need staff, materials, and working equipment. Either side can meet those needs by trading with the other.

So the statement is True.

Limited resources force careful choices — that is scarcity, and economising is the response. Assuming unlimited supply would ignore the constraint the chapter starts from.

So the statement is True.

title: Households, entrepreneurs, and everyday exchange
context: Analyze the roles of households and entrepreneurs in everyday exchange of goods and services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Only consumers ever exchange goods; businesses are legally barred from all trade with households.
Only individual consumers have needs; registered businesses operate with zero internal needs of their own.
Choosing to keep pocket money unspent means a teenager has avoided making any economic decision.
Exchange is one way needs and wants get fulfilled when households and businesses trade with each other.
Because money is used, barter arrangements can never count as genuine exchange.
tactical_explanations:
Businesses trade with households every day — selling goods, buying labour, hiring suppliers. There is no legal bar that confines exchange to consumers alone.

So the statement is False.

A shop needs stock, premises, and staff just as a family needs food and heat. Registered businesses are not need-free shells.

So the statement is False.

Leaving pocket money unspent is still a choice about scarce cash — save now, spend later, or hold it. The teenager has not stepped outside economic decision-making.

So the statement is False.

When a household pays a firm (or another household) for something useful, exchange is doing the work of fulfilling a need or want.

So the statement is True.

Barter is exchange without money: gardening help for a bookshelf still swaps valued things. Cash is common, not required.

So the statement is False.

title: Business Operations and Institutional Needs
context: Consider households, startups, and manufacturing firms interacting in a market system. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Businesses provide goods like computers and services like installing software for people to satisfy their needs.
Manufacturers of smartphones may have an operational need for electronic components produced by specialised suppliers.
To fabricate components, a manufacturer requires raw materials and a workforce rather than operating in isolation.
Individuals frequently exchange goods and services directly and are fully active participants in trading.
Households need food, shelter, and medical care, and they also want leisure activities such as cinema visits.
tactical_explanations:
Computers are goods; installing software is a service — both help people meet needs.

So the statement is True.

A smartphone maker cannot assemble handsets without specialised electronic parts from suppliers. That input requirement is an operational need of the manufacturer.

So the statement is True.

Fabricating components means drawing on raw materials and a workforce; isolation is not how production works.

So the statement is True.

People buy, sell, and swap goods and services directly — they are full participants in trade, not spectators.

So the statement is True.

Food, shelter, and medical care are household needs; cinema nights are wants layered on top. Both sit inside everyday household demand.

So the statement is True.

title: Corner café: beans and cappuccinos
context: Consider a corner café where customers buy bags of coffee beans and pay baristas to prepare drinks. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bag of roasted beans is a good and the barista's drink preparation is a service.
Needs and wants are identical concepts, so there is no meaningful difference between craving caffeine and a flavoured latte.
A habitual craving for a particular drink is more accurately a want if it is not essential for basic well-being.
Because the café is a business, it cannot itself be said to have needs such as reliable suppliers.
Paying for beans or drinks fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides of the transaction.
tactical_explanations:
Roasted beans in a bag are a tangible good; the barista’s drink preparation is an intangible service.

So the statement is True.

Needing enough caffeine to function is not the same as craving a flavoured latte for pleasure. Needs cover basic well-being; wants cover non-essential desires — the concepts are not identical.

So the statement is False.

A habitual favourite drink that is not essential for survival or basic health sits in the want category.

So the statement is True.

The café needs reliable bean suppliers, cups, and staff hours to keep serving customers. Being a business does not wipe those operational needs away.

So the statement is False.

Customer pays, café supplies — each side gets something valued. That two-sided fulfilment is exchange.

So the statement is True.

title: Jonas: bus pass or game skin
context: Consider jonas has twelve euros pocket money and must choose between an eight-euro bus pass and a ten-euro game skin. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bus pass is a need for getting to school, while the game skin is a want rather than a basic necessity.
Because both items have a price, they must both be classified as needs rather than wants.
Individuals face economic decisions about scarce resources even before they run a business or register as entrepreneurs.
Choosing to save the twelve euros and buy nothing means Jonas has opted out of all economic decision-making.
Once Jonas buys the bus pass, his want for the game skin permanently disappears and can never return.
tactical_explanations:
Getting to school with the bus pass supports a need; the game skin is entertainment, not a basic necessity.

So the statement is True.

Price tags do not turn wants into needs. A ten-euro skin remains a want even though it costs money. Classification rests on necessity for well-being, not on whether something is sold.

So the statement is False.

Jonas’s twelve-euro choice already forces trade-offs among the bus pass, the game skin, and saving — before any business registration enters the picture.

So the statement is False.

Saving the twelve euros is itself an allocation: hold cash now rather than buy the pass or the skin. Choosing not to buy is not escaping economics; it is one use of limited means.

So the statement is False.

Buying the bus pass does not delete the desire for the game skin. The want can return next month with new pocket money. “Permanently” and “never” overclaim.

So the statement is False.

title: PhoneFix screen repairs
context: Consider phoneFix Wien replaces cracked screens using spare parts ordered in limited monthly batches. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Screen replacement is a service, while a phone case sold at the counter is a good.
Because PhoneFix is a business rather than a household, its monthly spare parts can never run scarce.
A customer buying a decorative case purely for its design is satisfying a want rather than a basic need.
Repairing a phone never fulfils a need because phones are luxury items outside normal economic analysis.
A limited monthly batch of parts forces the shop to economise by prioritising which jobs to accept.
tactical_explanations:
Screen replacement is labour on the customer’s device — a service. A phone case sold at the counter is a tangible take-away — a good.

So the statement is True.

A limited monthly parts batch is scarce by definition: once it is gone, further repairs wait. Calling the shop a business does not create an infinite stockroom.

So the statement is False.

A decorative case bought only for its look is preference, not a requirement for basic well-being — a want.

So the statement is True.

Whether someone casually calls phones a luxury, repair can still meet a real need — school contact, work, emergencies. Phones are not outside economic analysis, and “never” is too strong.

So the statement is False.

A fixed monthly parts batch is a hard capacity ceiling. The shop must decide which jobs to take, delay, or refuse — that ranking is economising.

So the statement is True.

title: Defining the economy from scratch
context: Consider during a first lesson students list core building blocks of economic life. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The economy consists essentially of households and entrepreneurs interacting with one another.
Goods are tangible items, whereas services are intangible activities performed for someone.
Both households and businesses have needs, and exchange is one way those needs and wants get fulfilled.
Scarcity forces individuals and businesses to economise rather than assume unlimited resources.
Nobody, whether a household or a business, can truly opt out of making economic decisions.
tactical_explanations:
Introductory models summarise the economy as households and entrepreneurs interacting through exchange.

So the statement is True.

Goods are tangible items; services are intangible activities performed for someone.

So the statement is True.

Both households and businesses have needs (and wants). Trading with others is one way those get fulfilled.

So the statement is True.

Scarcity means resources are limited relative to desired uses. Economising is the careful response; assuming unlimited means denies the constraint.

So the statement is True.

Every actor still faces scarce time and limited means. Trying to “opt out” leaves those constraints in place — including the decision to do nothing with a resource.

So the statement is True.

title: Herr Novak's bakery
context: Consider herr Novak sells bread at his Linz bakery and charges one euro extra for doorstep delivery. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Herr Novak acts as an entrepreneur, while the families buying his bread act as households.
Bread is a good and doorstep delivery is a service, matching the distinction between tangible and intangible offerings.
Because Herr Novak owns a business, he personally has no needs of his own.
Paying for delivery is not exchange because a service has no monetary value once it has been performed.
Flour and oven fuel are unlimited for any bakery, so Herr Novak never has to economise on ingredients.
tactical_explanations:
Herr Novak organises production and sale at the bakery — entrepreneur. Families buying bread act as households.

So the statement is True.

Bread is a tangible good; doorstep delivery is an intangible service. Tangible versus activity matches the usual split.

So the statement is True.

Owning a bakery does not cancel Herr Novak’s personal needs for food, housing, or rest. Entrepreneur role and private household needs coexist in the same person.

So the statement is False.

Paying one euro extra for delivery is still a swap of money for a valued service. Performance ending does not erase the exchange that just occurred.

So the statement is False.

Flour and oven fuel arrive in limited quantities and at a cost. A bakery must choose batch sizes and recipes under those limits — that is economising.

So the statement is False.

title: Exchange without money
context: Assess statements about exchange, barter, and fulfilling needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Two neighbours swapping gardening lessons for a handmade bookshelf still counts as exchange even without money.
Exchange can only occur when euro banknotes or electronic transfers are used between the parties.
Wood used to build the bookshelf is a limited resource, so the carpenter must economise on how much he uses.
Gardening lessons are a service because they are an activity performed for the neighbour, not a physical item.
Individuals, not only businesses, have needs and wants that direct exchange can help satisfy.
tactical_explanations:
Gardening lessons for a handmade bookshelf is a clear swap of valued things. Money is absent; exchange is not.

So the statement is True.

Euro notes and bank transfers are convenient media of exchange, not the definition of it. Two neighbours can still trade lessons for furniture with no cash changing hands. Requiring banknotes would wrongly exclude barter from economics.

So the statement is False.

Wood for the bookshelf is finite. Using more on one project leaves less for the next — the carpenter must economise.

So the statement is True.

Gardening lessons are an activity performed for the neighbour, not a physical object handed over — a service.

So the statement is True.

People have needs and wants whether or not they run a firm.

So the statement is True.

title: Petra's dining table commission
context: Consider petra pays carpenter Fabian 650 euros for an oak dining table he builds and delivers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Petra's family acts as a household and Fabian acts as an entrepreneur in this transaction.
The finished dining table is a good because it is a tangible item Fabian produces and delivers.
Paying for the table fulfils the family's need for furniture through exchange.
Fabian has no genuine need for timber because raw materials are merely wants for any business.
Timber is a limited resource, so Fabian must economise on how much oak he uses per commission.
tactical_explanations:
Petra’s family buys as a household; Fabian builds and sells as an entrepreneur.

So the statement is True.

The finished oak table is a tangible item Fabian produces and delivers — a good.

So the statement is True.

Paying €650 for the table is exchange that meets the family’s furniture need.

So the statement is True.

Timber is an operational input Fabian must obtain to keep building. Calling raw materials “merely wants” mislabels a production need. Without oak he cannot deliver the commissioned table at all.

So the statement is False.

Oak is limited and costly. Fabian has to plan how much board goes into each commission rather than cut freely.

So the statement is True.

title: Needs, wants, and who has them
context: Analyze claims about needs, wants, and which actors in the economy face them. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A manufacturer of laptops may need specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production running.
High-tech manufacturers have zero internal needs because only end consumers ever experience genuine need.
Households buy goods and services from businesses to satisfy both needs and wants in daily life.
Wants disappear automatically once every need has been fully satisfied in a given month.
Teenagers with pocket money are outside the economy until they register a business or join a formal household.
tactical_explanations:
Without specialised electronic parts from suppliers, laptop production stalls.

So the statement is True.

High-tech firms need components, energy, and skilled staff just as consumers need goods. “Zero internal needs” is wrong.

So the statement is False.

Daily shopping — food, transport, streaming, clothes — is households using market exchange for both needs and wants.

So the statement is True.

Satisfying food and rent for one month does not switch off desires for holidays, gadgets, or better housing. Wants keep regenerating; they are not a one-time checklist that disappears when basics are covered.

So the statement is False.

Teenagers with pocket money already buy, save, and trade. They sit on the household side long before any business registration.

So the statement is False.

title: Lukas end-of-month pocket money
context: Consider student Lukas has 300 euros monthly for transport, toiletries, and designer trainers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Ninety euros for transport and toiletries covers needs, while 140-euro trainers cover a want.
Because Lukas receives money from parents, he is not part of the household side of the economy.
Buying trainers makes his need for transport disappear for the rest of the month.
Wanting trainers is irrational and therefore falls outside the scope of economics entirely.
A fixed monthly sum is an unlimited resource that never needs to be economised.
tactical_explanations:
Transport and toiletries support everyday functioning — needs. Designer trainers at €140 are desired extras — a want.

So the statement is True.

Money from parents places Lukas inside a household budget.

So the statement is False.

Buying trainers spends part of the month’s cash; it does not cancel the need to get to school. Transport still has to be covered from whatever remains of the €300 — the want purchase does not erase the need.

So the statement is False.

Economics studies how people allocate scarce means among competing ends — including wants. Calling trainers “irrational” does not eject them from the subject.

So the statement is False.

Three hundred euros a month is a hard ceiling. Choosing trainers versus transport is economising, not swimming in unlimited means.

So the statement is False.

title: Farmer Reinisch's market stall
context: Consider farmer Reinisch sells potatoes and carrots from eight hectares at a Saturday village market. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Reinisch acts as an entrepreneur at the stall while village buyers act as households.
Because farmland can theoretically be bought elsewhere, Reinisch's eight hectares should not be treated as scarce.
Potatoes and carrots are goods rather than services even though they must be cooked before eating.
Splitting eight hectares between crops is an economic decision Reinisch cannot avoid given limited land.
Paying cash at the stall is not genuine exchange because only barter counts as real economic trade.
tactical_explanations:
Reinisch sells produce as an entrepreneur; village buyers act as households at the stall.

So the statement is True.

Eight hectares on this farm are the land he actually commands. Theoretical land elsewhere does not make his own plot non-scarce.

So the statement is False.

Potatoes and carrots are tangible items. Needing cooking before eating does not turn them into services.

So the statement is True.

Limited land means crop mix is a forced allocation decision — Reinisch cannot plant everything on the same hectares.

So the statement is True.

Cash payment is the usual form of exchange at a market stall. Barter is one form of trade, not the only valid one.

So the statement is False.

title: Market day in Hallstatt
context: Consider toni sells cheese wheels; Rosa offers children's face-painting; families buy for groceries or fun. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Toni and Rosa act as entrepreneurs while visiting families act as households.
A cheese wheel is a good and face-painting is a service.
Buying cheese for weekly groceries satisfies a need, while face-painting satisfies more of a want.
Paying for cheese or face-painting fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides.
Because Toni has only thirty wheels left, he must economise by allocating stock among queuing families.
tactical_explanations:
Toni and Rosa organise offerings for sale — entrepreneurs. Visiting families buy as households.

So the statement is True.

A cheese wheel is a good; face-painting is a service.

So the statement is True.

Weekly grocery cheese supports a need; face-painting is enjoyment rather than basic well-being — more of a want.

So the statement is True.

Money for cheese or for face-painting is exchange: each side gives something and receives something valued.

So the statement is True.

Thirty wheels left is a hard stock limit on market day. Toni must decide how many to hold for regulars, how many to sell early, and whom to turn away when the queue outruns the crate — that ranking is economising under scarcity.

So the statement is True.

title: Scarcity across actors
context: Assess whether scarcity and economising apply uniformly. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A multinational corporation with large cash reserves still faces scarce managerial attention and factory capacity.
Households never economise because their wants are unlimited and budgets therefore do not constrain them.
Governments are excluded from scarcity because they can always raise taxes to fund any project immediately.
Economising is rational behaviour when a resource is limited relative to competing uses.
Entrepreneurs must economise on inputs such as labour hours and raw materials to stay viable.
tactical_explanations:
Large cash reserves do not create infinite managerial attention or factory hours. Those remain scarce even for a multinational.

So the statement is True.

Unlimited wants are exactly why budgets bite.

So the statement is False.

Raising taxes takes political time and still claims finite real resources — labour, materials, administrative capacity. A government cannot fund every project “immediately” just by changing a tax rate. Scarcity binds the public sector too.

So the statement is False.

When a resource has competing uses and is limited, careful allocation — economising — is the rational response.

So the statement is True.

Labour hours and raw materials cost money and run out. Entrepreneurs who ignore that constraint do not stay viable.

So the statement is True.

title: Kaffee Ecke morning queue
context: Consider owner Sami sells bean bags and employs baristas; a rare Ethiopian lot is limited to forty kilograms. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Sami supplies goods and services as an entrepreneur while customers act as households.
The bean bag is a good and espresso preparation is a service.
A strong habitual coffee craving may reflect a want rather than a strict survival need.
Trying a new seasonal flavour for enjoyment is best classified as a want.
The forty-kilogram cap forces Sami to economise on how he allocates beans across the season.
tactical_explanations:
Sami sells beans and drinks as an entrepreneur; customers buy as households.

So the statement is True.

A bag of beans is a good; pulling an espresso is a service performed for the customer.

So the statement is True.

A strong coffee habit can be comfort or preference rather than a strict survival requirement — often a want.

So the statement is True.

Trying a new seasonal flavour for enjoyment is desire, not basic necessity — a want.

So the statement is True.

Forty kilograms of the rare lot is a hard season cap. Sami must decide which drinks and bag sales get that coffee — economising under the limit.

So the statement is True.

title: Classmates swap novels for algebra help
context: Consider nora lends Felix novels; Felix tutors her two afternoons with no money exchanged. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Exchange requires money, so this novels-for-tutoring swap does not count as exchange at all.
Felix's tutoring is a service and Nora's novels are goods, matching the standard classification.
Because both are students rather than businesses, needs, wants, and exchange concepts do not apply.
Felix's limited free time is a scarce resource allocated between tutoring and his other commitments.
Once the swap is agreed, both have opted out of any further economic decisions about their time.
tactical_explanations:
Novels for algebra tutoring is still a mutual swap of valued things. Money is not required for exchange.

So the statement is False.

Felix’s tutoring is an activity — a service. Nora’s novels are tangible goods. The labels line up.

So the statement is True.

Students still have scarce time, needs, and wants. Being classmates rather than firms does not eject them from exchange concepts.

So the statement is False.

Felix’s free afternoons are limited. Tutoring Nora means fewer hours for homework, sport, or rest — allocation of a scarce resource.

So the statement is True.

After the swap, both still decide how to use remaining evenings, weekends, and energy. Agreement on one trade is not a full exit from economic choices.

So the statement is False.

title: Opting out of the economy?
context: Analyze whether households or businesses can successfully opt out of economic decisions. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Retired couples growing their own food still face scarcity of land, time, and seed and must economise.
Repairing a customer's bicycle at a workshop is a service because it is work performed rather than an item handed over.
Selling surplus eggs to neighbours for cash is exchange that fulfils buyers' needs or wants.
Because retirees no longer earn wages, they must be classified as entrepreneurs rather than households.
Deciding how much land to plant versus how many chickens to keep is an unavoidable economic choice.
tactical_explanations:
Growing your own food still uses limited land, time, and seed. Retirees must choose plot layouts and crop mixes — economising continues.

So the statement is True.

Bicycle repair is work performed on the customer’s bike — a service.

So the statement is True.

Surplus eggs sold for cash give neighbours food and the seller money. That trade fulfils needs or wants through exchange.

So the statement is True.

Stopping wage work does not turn retirees into entrepreneurs by default. They typically remain households. Selling the occasional surplus egg does not automatically reclassify them as firms organising production under uncertainty.

So the statement is False.

Land planted in vegetables cannot also hold the same square metres of chicken run. The mix is an unavoidable allocation choice under scarce space.

So the statement is True.

title: Remote cabin and firewood trade
context: Consider karl lives in a remote cabin and occasionally trades firewood for canned food from hikers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The occasional firewood-for-food trade is exchange fulfilling needs even without shops nearby.
Because Karl avoids shops, he has genuinely opted out of making economic decisions.
Karl's claim that he needs nobody proves scarcity no longer applies to him personally.
Chopping firewood requires no economising because forests are unlimited resources for anyone living remotely.
Only members of registered businesses or official households are affected by needs, wants, and scarcity.
tactical_explanations:
Firewood for canned food is exchange that meets needs even far from shops.

So the statement is True.

Avoiding shops does not cancel decisions about time, firewood, and food stocks. Karl still chooses under scarcity.

So the statement is False.

Claiming “I need nobody” does not create infinite wood, daylight, or energy. Scarcity still binds his daily work.

So the statement is False.

Forests regenerate slowly and chopping takes time and tools. Remote living does not make timber an unlimited free flow.

So the statement is False.

Needs, wants, and scarcity apply to people generally. A cabin dweller trading with hikers still faces limited daylight for chopping and limited shelf space for cans — formal registration is irrelevant to those constraints.

So the statement is False.

title: Electrician Boris and the Hoffmanns
context: Consider the Hoffmanns pay Boris 180 euros for kitchen wiring; that evening Boris buys groceries for his family. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The Hoffmanns act as a household paying for repair; Boris acts as an entrepreneur supplying it.
Electrical repair is a service because it is work performed rather than a physical item delivered.
Faulty wiring created a need for a working system fulfilled through exchange of money for service.
When Boris buys groceries later, he acts as a household with needs of his own.
Boris's limited working hours are a scarce resource he must economise across jobs.
tactical_explanations:
The Hoffmanns pay for kitchen wiring as a household; Boris supplies the repair as an entrepreneur.

So the statement is True.

Electrical repair is labour performed, not a boxed product delivered — a service.

So the statement is True.

Faulty wiring created a need for a safe working system; paying Boris meets that need through exchange.

So the statement is True.

Buying groceries that evening, Boris spends as a household with his own family’s needs — roles can switch across the day.

So the statement is True.

Working hours are finite. Accepting one job means less time for another; Boris must economise across bookings.

So the statement is True.

title: Goods versus services traps
context: Review subtle classification traps distinguishing goods from services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Installing software on a customer's computer is a service, not a good, even though it involves a physical machine.
A downloadable e-book file is a service because it has no weight and therefore cannot be a good.
Only goods, never services, can be exchanged in a market between households and firms.
A restaurant meal eaten on the premises is a good because food is always tangible.
Delivery of a pizza to a customer's door converts the pizza from a service into a good.
tactical_explanations:
Installing software is an activity performed for the customer. The computer’s physical presence does not turn the install into a good.

So the statement is True.

An e-book file is a digital good — an item that can be owned and transferred — even though it has no weight. Lack of mass does not force the service label.

So the statement is False.

Haircuts, repairs, lessons, and installs are exchanged every day between households and firms. Services trade in markets too.

So the statement is False.

A meal on the premises mixes food with preparation and serving. Calling the whole experience “a good because food is tangible” ignores the service element restaurants sell.

So the statement is False.

Delivery is an extra service layered onto the pizza. The pizza remains a good; the drop-off does not rewrite its category.

So the statement is False.

title: Street musician tips
context: Consider elena busks on the main square; listeners drop coins into her case for violin performances. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Elena's performance is a service because it is an activity enjoyed rather than a physical item handed over.
Listeners paying because they enjoy the atmosphere are satisfying a want rather than a basic survival need.
Because each tip amount is voluntary and unfixed, no exchange takes place between Elena and the listeners.
Elena's need to cover rent shows that individuals, not only registered businesses, experience economic needs.
Elena's limited performing time each Sunday is a scarce resource she must economise across locations.
tactical_explanations:
Elena’s violin performance is an activity listeners enjoy — a service.

So the statement is True.

Paying for atmosphere and music is enjoyment rather than survival — a want.

So the statement is True.

A tip still swaps money for a performance the listener values. Voluntary and unfixed amounts do not cancel exchange; street music funded by coins in a case is still trade of money for a service.

So the statement is False.

Rent is a personal obligation. Elena’s need to cover it shows individuals face economic needs, not only registered firms.

So the statement is True.

Sunday hours are limited. Choosing one square over another allocates scarce performing time — economising.

So the statement is True.

title: Hair salon: cut versus shampoo
context: Consider sabine pays twenty-five euros for a haircut and may buy a shampoo bottle at the counter. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The haircut is a service and the shampoo bottle is a good.
Because Sabine pays for both with money, both must be classified as goods rather than services.
Timo the self-employed hairdresser has no needs of his own since he is on the entrepreneur side.
Sabine's regular six-week visits mean scarcity no longer applies because the purchase became routine.
Paying for either item still involves exchange that can fulfil a need or want.
tactical_explanations:
The haircut is labour performed — a service. The shampoo bottle is a tangible take-home product — a good.

So the statement is True.

Paying with money does not force both items into the goods column. Classification follows tangibility and activity, not the payment medium.

So the statement is False.

Self-employed Timo still needs food, housing, and rest as a person. Standing on the entrepreneur side of a trade does not erase private needs.

So the statement is False.

Routine six-week visits still use scarce money and chair time. Familiarity does not abolish scarcity.

So the statement is False.

Paying for the cut or the bottle is still exchange that can meet a need (grooming) or a want (a preferred brand).

So the statement is True.

title: Exchange breadth
context: Analyze how broadly exchange can occur between households and businesses. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Households exchange with firms when they buy groceries, and with other households when they sell used furniture.
Only entrepreneurs are entitled to exchange; households may consume but never trade.
Barter between two individuals still counts as exchange when each gives something the other values.
Exchange always requires a written contract registered with a government authority to be valid.
Paying with a mobile app transfer is exchange just like paying with coins or banknotes.
tactical_explanations:
Buying groceries is household–firm trade; selling used furniture to a neighbour is household–household trade.

So the statement is True.

Households trade constantly — shopping, selling used goods, hiring help. Exchange is not an entrepreneur-only privilege.

So the statement is False.

When each person gives something the other values, barter is exchange.

So the statement is True.

Most everyday trades need no registered written contract. Handshake sales, market-stall cash, and till receipts still count. Requiring government paperwork would erase nearly all ordinary exchange from the definition.

So the statement is False.

A mobile-app transfer moves purchasing power just as coins or banknotes do. The medium changes; the exchange does not.

So the statement is True.

title: Soup kitchen volunteers
context: Consider volunteers cook free soup using donated vegetables and a church kitchen lent at no charge. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Because soup is free, no recipient need is fulfilled and no exchange occurs in any sense.
Donated vegetables, kitchen time, and volunteer labour are limited and require economising.
Absence of money means volunteers and recipients have fully opted out of economic decisions.
Choosing which vegetables to use first is an unavoidable economic decision given limited supplies.
The church lending its kitchen has no needs of its own because it is not a for-profit business.
tactical_explanations:
Free soup still meets hunger. Recipients get a meal; volunteers and donors still allocate scarce vegetables, kitchen space, and time. “No price” is not “no need” and not “no exchange of effort for help.”

So the statement is False.

Donated vegetables, kitchen hours, and volunteer labour are finite. Someone still has to decide how much soup to cook and who gets a bowl first.

So the statement is True.

Skipping cash does not eject anyone from economics. Volunteers choose how long to stay; the church chooses whether to lend the kitchen; recipients queue and eat rather than walk away. Those are allocations of scarce time, space, and food even when no euro changes hands. A gift economy still forces ranking: which night to open, which stock to use, how many litres to prepare.

So the statement is False.

With a limited crate of vegetables, using carrots today means fewer carrots tomorrow. That ranking of scarce ingredients is an economic decision, money or not.

So the statement is True.

A church still needs a usable kitchen, volunteers, and donated stock to run the meal. Not-for-profit status does not cancel operational needs.

So the statement is False.

title: Needs of businesses
context: Review whether businesses themselves have operational needs in addition to household needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A smartphone assembler needs specialised electronic components from suppliers to manufacture devices.
Businesses have zero internal needs because only final consumers experience genuine need.
An entrepreneur needs customers and revenue to keep staff employed and operations running.
Operational needs of firms include workforce, premises, and raw materials, not only consumer demand.
If a firm is profitable, scarcity no longer applies to any of its inputs.
tactical_explanations:
Without specialised components from suppliers, the assembler cannot build phones. That input requirement is a genuine business need.

So the statement is True.

Final consumers are not the only agents with needs. Firms need parts, labour, premises, and working capital to operate at all. Treating business needs as “not genuine” confuses who feels the need with whether the need exists.

So the statement is False.

Staff wages and day-to-day running costs have to be covered. An entrepreneur who cannot attract customers or revenue cannot keep the operation alive, so customers and sales are operational needs, not optional extras.

So the statement is True.

Workforce, premises, and raw materials sit beside consumer demand as what the firm must secure to keep producing.

So the statement is True.

Profit means the firm earned a surplus last period; it does not make steel, electricity, or skilled hours suddenly infinite. A profitable assembler still queues for chips, still pays rent, and still schedules scarce machine time. Scarcity is about limited means relative to uses, not about whether the accounts show black ink.

So the statement is False.

title: Cannot opt out
context: Analyze the claim that nobody can fully opt out of making economic decisions. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Choosing to hoard cash under a mattress is still an economic decision about using a scarce resource.
Only people who run businesses make economic decisions; pure consumers never face scarcity.
Doing nothing with a weekly allowance is opting out of economics because no purchase occurred.
Retirees living on a pension no longer make economic decisions because income is guaranteed.
Children too young to earn wages are entirely outside economic life and never economise.
tactical_explanations:
Cash under the mattress is still a use of scarce purchasing power: held idle instead of spent, saved in a bank, or invested. That allocation is an economic decision even if no shop receipt appears.

So the statement is True.

Consumers face scarcity every time a budget cannot cover every shopping list item. Business ownership is not a ticket into economic life.

So the statement is False.

Leaving the weekly allowance untouched is still a choice about scarce money — keep it, spend it later, or give it away. “No purchase today” is not “outside economics”; inaction uses the same limited pot and forgoes other uses.

So the statement is False.

A pension is income, not a free pass from choice. Retirees still decide rent versus travel, insurance packages, and how much cash to hold. Guaranteed income changes the size of the budget, not the fact of scarce means.

So the statement is False.

Children economise toys, screen time, and shares of a snack long before they earn a wage. Formal employment is not the entry gate to economic life.

So the statement is False.

title: Household wants beyond basics
context: Assess the range of household needs and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Households need food, shelter, and medical care to maintain basic well-being.
Sports, cinema visits, and café outings are examples of wants rather than strict needs.
A household buying cinema tickets is satisfying a want through exchange with a business.
Households and entrepreneurs interact when families purchase goods and services from firms.
Limited household income forces economising between essential needs and discretionary wants.
tactical_explanations:
Food, shelter, and medical care underpin basic well-being; textbooks treat them as core household needs.

So the statement is True.

Sports, cinema, and café visits are desirable extras. Households can postpone or drop them without the same threat to survival that missing meals or housing would pose, so they sit in the want category.

So the statement is True.

Buying cinema tickets is a household want met by paying a cinema business — classic exchange.

So the statement is True.

Families purchase goods and services from firms; that is the everyday link between household demand and entrepreneurial supply.

So the statement is True.

A finite pay cheque cannot fund every need and every want at once. Households rank groceries against streaming, rent against a weekend away, and that ranking is economising under limited income.

So the statement is True.

title: Cerny family September budget
context: Consider the Cerny family has 1,400 euros after rent for groceries, school supplies, and an optional weekend trip. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Groceries and school supplies are needs, while the weekend trip is a want.
The fixed 1,400-euro remainder is a limited resource the household must economise.
School supplies bought for children count as needs of the household as a whole.
Deciding whether to book the trip is an economic decision because inaction is also a choice.
If the family skips the trip, their want for it is permanently erased and can never return.
tactical_explanations:
Groceries and school supplies support daily living and schooling; the optional weekend trip is a discretionary want.

So the statement is True.

After rent, 1,400 euros is the whole discretionary pot for food, supplies, and leisure. That ceiling forces trade-offs: more trip spending means tighter grocery or supply choices.

So the statement is True.

School supplies for the children are household needs even though the kids are not separate paying customers.

So the statement is True.

Booking or skipping the trip both use the same scarce remainder. Refusing the booking is still a decision about that 1,400 euros, not a walk-out from economics.

So the statement is True.

Skipping September’s trip does not delete the preference. Next month the family can want the same weekend away again; wants persist and reappear when budgets allow. Inaction postpones fulfilment; it does not erase the want forever.

So the statement is False.

title: Households and Entrepreneurs in Exchange
context: Analyze how households and entrepreneurs interact when goods and services change hands. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A family selling a used bicycle online remains a household even while acting as a seller.
Exchange requires identical needs on both sides before any trade can occur.
Only multinational corporations count as entrepreneurs under basic economic definitions.
Households supply finished goods to entrepreneurs while firms supply only unpaid advice.
Repair workshops are households because customers visit the premises in person.
tactical_explanations:
Selling a used bike online does not turn the family into a firm. They remain a household disposing of a personal good, even while they act as the seller in that one swap.

So the statement is True.

Trade needs complementary wants, not identical ones. One side wants the bike; the other wants the cash — that difference is why exchange happens.

So the statement is False.

Entrepreneur here means someone organising production or sale for the market — a neighbourhood café owner counts as much as a multinational. The label is about the role in exchange, not company size or border-crossing brands.

So the statement is False.

Usual flow is the reverse of the claim: households supply labour and buy finished goods; firms supply goods and services and buy labour and inputs. Unpaid advice is not what firms mainly deliver to households.

So the statement is False.

A repair workshop sells repair services for payment — that is an entrepreneurial business, not a household, even when customers walk in.

So the statement is False.

title: Mira's Market Lunch Choice
context: Consider Mira, who has fifteen euros for either a hot lunch or saving toward winter boots. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Mira's fifteen euros are a limited resource she must allocate between lunch today and future boot savings.
Once Mira buys lunch, scarcity disappears for the rest of the school term.
Choosing to save rather than eat out still counts as an economic decision about scarce money.
The hot lunch satisfies a need for nutrition while designer boots would reflect more of a want.
Only business owners participate in the economy; students with pocket money are excluded.
tactical_explanations:
Fifteen euros cannot buy lunch and fund the full boot pot at once. Mira has to split or dedicate that scarce cash.

So the statement is True.

Spending the fifteen euros on lunch closes that particular cash choice: those euros are no longer available for boots today.

So the statement is True.

Saving the money instead of eating out is still allocating scarce euros — toward boots later rather than lunch now. No receipt does not mean no economic decision.

So the statement is True.

A hot lunch covers nutrition, a basic need. Designer boots are typically a style want beyond bare footwear necessity, so the contrast in the claim fits the needs-versus-wants split.

So the statement is True.

Students with pocket money buy lunches, save, and trade second-hand goods. They participate as households (or young consumers) under scarcity. Owning a business is not required to be inside the economy.

So the statement is False.

title: Goods Versus Services Distinctions
context: Review how economists classify tangible goods and intangible services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A restaurant meal consumed on the premises combines goods with the service of preparation and serving.
Installing a heat pump in a home is a service even though the pump itself is a capital good.
Legal advice becomes a good once the lawyer writes a fee invoice.
Digital delivery automatically converts every product into a tangible good.
Textbooks are services because knowledge inside them is intangible.
tactical_explanations:
The plate of food is a tangible good; cooking and serving are services. A restaurant meal on the premises is therefore a bundle of both.

So the statement is True.

Installation labour is the service; the heat pump hardware is the capital good being fitted. The act of installing remains a service.

So the statement is True.

An invoice is just the bill for the advice. Writing a fee note does not freeze intangible counsel into a tangible good; legal advice stays a service whether or not paper accompanies payment.

So the statement is False.

Delivery channel does not rewrite the product type. A streamed film is still a service access; an e-book file can be a digital good. “Digital” alone never forces every product into tangible-good status.

So the statement is False.

A textbook is a physical (or digital) good you can hold or store. Intangible knowledge content does not turn the book itself into a service.

So the statement is False.

title: Needs, Wants, and Well-Being
context: Analyze how needs differ from wants when households and firms plan spending. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A teenager saving for concert tickets is pursuing a want rather than a basic need.
Weekend cinema tickets and premium streaming subscriptions typically reflect wants rather than strict needs.
Shelter, food, and basic healthcare are commonly treated as needs for household well-being.
Distinguishing needs from wants helps explain why households economise when budgets cannot cover everything.
Businesses may want brand recognition even while they need reliable suppliers to keep production running.
tactical_explanations:
Concert tickets are leisure spending. They sit with wants, not with food, shelter, or basic medical care.

So the statement is True.

Weekend cinema and premium streaming are enjoyable extras. Households can cut them when budgets tighten without the same damage as cutting essentials, so they read as wants.

So the statement is True.

Shelter, food, and basic healthcare are the standard examples of needs for household well-being.

So the statement is True.

When income cannot cover every line item, sorting needs from wants explains which purchases get priority and which get postponed — that is economising in practice.

So the statement is True.

A firm can chase brand recognition as a want while still needing dependable suppliers to keep lines running. Businesses carry both categories: operational needs for survival of production, and wants for image or expansion frills.

So the statement is True.

title: Bergwerk Farm Stall Exchange
context: Consider Bergwerk Farm, where Clara sells eggs and trades surplus vegetables with a neighbouring beekeeper. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Trading vegetables for honey without money still counts as exchange between economic actors.
Buyers at the stall act as households when they purchase eggs for family meals.
Clara must economise on feed and labour because her flock size and hours are limited.
Farm stall operators are consumers only because they grow food for themselves.
Barter can never satisfy needs because no price tag is attached.
tactical_explanations:
Vegetables for honey is barter: each side gives up something scarce and gains something valued. Money is optional for exchange.

So the statement is True.

Stall customers buying eggs for family meals are acting in the household role — acquiring food for private consumption, not organising a farm business.

So the statement is True.

Feed bags and daylight hours are limited. Clara cannot run an unlimited flock on unlimited labour, so she economises feed and time against flock size.

So the statement is True.

Clara grows and sells; that selling role is entrepreneurial. Growing some food for herself does not cancel the producer-seller side of the stall. Operators are not “consumers only.”

So the statement is False.

Barter can fill the fridge and the honey jar. Needs are met by what is received, not by whether a euro price tag was printed.

So the statement is False.

title: Scarcity and Economising Behaviour
context: Review why scarcity forces households and businesses to economise on resources. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Scarcity means available resources are limited relative to what decision-makers would like to use.
A bakery economises when it schedules oven use to avoid wasting flour and fuel on unsold loaves.
Even wealthy households economise when choosing how to allocate time among competing activities.
Governments never economise because taxation can fund every project simultaneously.
Economising means avoiding all spending until resources become literally infinite.
tactical_explanations:
Scarcity is the gap between limited means and unlimited preferred uses — exactly that relative limit.

So the statement is True.

Scheduling oven slots so flour and fuel are not burned on loaves that will not sell is classic economising: stretch scarce inputs toward profitable output.

So the statement is True.

Wealth does not create a second Tuesday. Rich households still choose among leisure, work, and family time because hours remain limited.

So the statement is True.

Tax revenue is large but finite within a budget year. Funding every project at once would require infinite means; governments still rank roads against hospitals and delay some schemes. Taxation reallocates scarce funds; it does not abolish scarcity.

So the statement is False.

Economising is careful spending and ranking under limits, not a strike until resources become infinite — an impossible waiting game.

So the statement is False.

title: Opting Out of Economic Decisions
context: Analyze whether any household or business can fully avoid economic decision-making. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A retiree choosing between medical insurance plans faces economic decisions despite receiving a pension.
Businesses that pause hiring still make an economic decision about how to use limited payroll budgets.
Only spending money counts as an economic decision; saving is excluded.
Children are outside economics until they earn a formal wage.
Religious communities opt out of economics by avoiding shops entirely.
tactical_explanations:
Pension income still leaves a menu of insurance plans with different premiums and cover. Choosing among them allocates scarce money and manages risk — textbook economic decisions in retirement.

So the statement is True.

Pausing hiring is a deliberate use of a limited payroll budget: keep cash, stretch existing staff, or wait. That freeze is itself a decision.

So the statement is True.

Saving parks purchasing power for later uses. Holding or depositing money is an allocation of scarce funds just as spending is. Economics covers both sides of the wallet, not only the checkout.

So the statement is False.

Before any wage, children choose among snacks, chores, and playtime. Formal pay is irrelevant to whether scarce toys or hours force economising.

So the statement is False.

Avoiding shops still leaves choices about donated food, shared space, and volunteer hours. Religious communities allocate scarce means inside and outside markets.

So the statement is False.

title: Exchange Mechanisms and Participants
context: Review who may exchange goods and services and through which mechanisms. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Exchange helps fulfil needs and wants on both sides when each party values what it receives.
Households may exchange with other households when selling second-hand furniture locally.
Barter between classmates swapping revision notes for borrowed textbooks is exchange without money.
Entrepreneurs exchange with other entrepreneurs when a café buys beans from a wholesale roaster.
Paying with a contactless card for groceries is exchange between a household and a supermarket entrepreneur.
tactical_explanations:
Each side values what it gets more than what it gives up; that mutual valuation is how exchange advances needs and wants.

So the statement is True.

A household selling used furniture to a neighbour is household-to-household exchange. Entrepreneur status is not required on both sides.

So the statement is True.

Notes for textbooks is a swap of scarce study resources without cash — barter, and still exchange.

So the statement is True.

A café buying beans from a roaster is firm-to-firm trade: entrepreneurs exchanging with entrepreneurs.

So the statement is True.

Contactless grocery payment is still a household handing purchasing power to a supermarket business for goods. The card is only the payment tool; the roles remain household and entrepreneur.

So the statement is True.

title: Taxi Fleet Owner Morning Shift
context: Consider a taxi fleet owner who assigns each vehicle either to airport runs or city-centre fares for the morning peak. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Fuel and driver wages are limited resources the owner must economise across the shift.
Route choice involves no trade-offs because both areas generate identical profit.
Fleet owners are households because they also drive passengers personally.
Fleet vehicles face no scarcity because engines can run whenever fuel is available.
Every passenger must register as an entrepreneur before entering a taxi.
tactical_explanations:
Fuel tanks and wage budgets are limited for the morning peak; the owner must stretch both across assigned runs.

So the statement is True.

Airport and city-centre work differ in fare mix, dead mileage, and waiting time. Sending a cab one way forgoes the other — a trade-off even when both look profitable on average.

So the statement is False.

Owning and deploying a fleet for paid rides is an entrepreneurial role. Personally taking a shift now and then does not redefine the fleet business as a household.

So the statement is False.

Engines need fuel, drivers, and maintenance slots. “Fuel exists somewhere” does not mean every vehicle can run every route at once without scarce diesel and labour.

So the statement is False.

Passengers are customers buying a ride service; they need not register as entrepreneurs to sit in the back seat.

So the statement is False.

title: Operational Needs of Businesses
context: Analyze whether firms and entrepreneurs experience genuine needs beyond consumer demand. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Cash flow to pay suppliers next month is a need for a small retailer even when sales are seasonal.
Customer demand itself can be a need when a firm requires sales to remain viable.
A laptop assembler needs specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production lines running.
An entrepreneur needs reliable staff and premises to continue serving paying customers.
Expansion plans and wage bills are identical categories with no distinction.
tactical_explanations:
Seasonal sales still leave supplier invoices due next month. Cash to meet those bills is an operational need for the retailer, not a luxury.

So the statement is True.

Without enough sales, the firm cannot fund wages and stock. Demand can therefore be a need for viability, not only a want for growth.

So the statement is True.

Specialised components are required inputs; without them the assembly line stops.

So the statement is True.

Reliable staff and usable premises are what let the entrepreneur keep serving paying customers day after day.

So the statement is True.

Expansion plans are forward-looking wants or strategic aims; the wage bill is a recurring operational claim on cash. Mixing them as “identical categories” blurs needs of running the firm with optional growth projects.

So the statement is False.

title: Digital Subscription Household
context: Consider the Hofer family comparing one combined streaming bundle against separate music and film subscriptions within a fixed monthly budget. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Paying the monthly fee is exchange with the streaming company acting as entrepreneur.
The Hofer family acts as a household allocating a limited entertainment budget among subscriptions.
Premium sports channels reflect more of a want than basic news coverage for household well-being.
Choosing the bundle over separate plans still involves economising because the budget cannot fund every option.
Digital files are always goods because they can be downloaded to a device.
tactical_explanations:
The monthly fee pays a streaming firm for access — household–entrepreneur exchange.

So the statement is True.

The Hofers are allocating a capped entertainment budget across bundle versus separate plans. That household role is exactly budgeted choice under a limit.

So the statement is True.

Premium sports add leisure enjoyment; basic news is closer to everyday information needs. The sports tier sits further toward wants.

So the statement is True.

Even the cheaper-looking bundle uses part of a budget that cannot also fund every separate add-on. Ranking options is still economising.

So the statement is True.

Downloadability does not settle the goods-versus-services line. Many digital offers are access services (streaming rights); some downloads behave more like digital goods. “Can sit on a device” alone does not make every file a good.

So the statement is False.

title: Scarcity Across Actor Types
context: Assess whether scarcity applies uniformly to households, firms, and governments. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A multinational firm with large reserves still faces scarce factory capacity and managerial attention.
Local councils splitting a fixed parks budget face scarcity similar in kind to household budget choices.
Households with modest incomes economise when choosing between rent, food, and transport each month.
Students have unlimited time because weekends repeat every week.
Rising input prices remove scarcity because suppliers always deliver more.
tactical_explanations:
Cash reserves do not multiply factory floors or CEO hours. Capacity and attention remain scarce even inside a large multinational.

So the statement is True.

A fixed parks budget forces the same kind of ranking households know: more for one park means less for another.

So the statement is True.

Modest income means rent, food, and transport compete for the same euros each month — everyday household economising under scarcity.

So the statement is True.

Weekends recur, but each weekend is still only two days. Exam weeks, jobs, and sleep crowd the same calendar; repeating the label “weekend” does not create unlimited study hours.

So the statement is False.

Higher input prices often tighten scarcity: the same budget buys fewer units. Suppliers do not automatically ship infinite extra volume just because prices rose.

So the statement is False.

title: Community Garden Plot Allocation
context: Consider twenty household plots sharing one water tap on scheduled mornings at a community garden. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Each gardener acts partly as a household producer deciding how to use a small allocated bed.
Neighbour swaps are friendship only and never count as exchange.
Large outdoor space removes the need to choose among crops.
Only purchases in shops count as economic decisions for gardeners.
Community gardens eliminate scarcity because soil is outdoors.
tactical_explanations:
Each plot holder decides crops and watering for a small bed serving the household — a household-producer role on allocated land.

So the statement is True.

Swapping tomatoes for herbs is still giving up one scarce harvest for another. Friendship may motivate the deal; the swap itself is exchange.

So the statement is False.

Outdoor space does not erase bed size, sunlight, or the single shared tap. Twenty plots still cannot each grow every crop at once; gardeners choose among plantings.

So the statement is False.

Choosing watering slots, crop mix, and whether to trade surplus are economic decisions at the garden gate, not only at the supermarket till.

So the statement is False.

Outdoor soil is still limited in area, nutrients, and water access. “Outside” does not cancel scarcity.

So the statement is False.

title: Household and Entrepreneur Roles Combined
context: Review situations where the same person acts as household member and entrepreneur. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A freelance designer invoicing a client acts as an entrepreneur during that project.
Exchange occurs when the designer is paid by a corporate client and when later paying a baker.
Needs in the business role include software licences; wants may include a premium portfolio website.
The same designer buying groceries after work acts as a household in the supermarket.
Both roles involve decisions under scarce resources such as time, money, and skills.
tactical_explanations:
Invoicing a client for design work is selling a service on the market — the entrepreneur role for that project.

So the statement is True.

Payment from the corporate client is exchange in the business role; paying the baker later is exchange in the household role. Same person, two market sides across the day.

So the statement is True.

Software licences keep the freelance business able to deliver — a need. A premium portfolio site is a desirable upgrade — more of a want.

So the statement is True.

Buying groceries after work is ordinary household consumption, not entrepreneurship.

So the statement is True.

Billable hours, cash, and skills are limited whether the person is quoting a client or shopping for dinner. Both roles force ranking under scarcity.

So the statement is True.

title: Classification Traps for Goods and Services
context: Evaluate subtle classification claims about goods, services, needs, and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A luxury handbag purchase primarily satisfies a want rather than a basic household need.
A bus ticket granting transport right is often treated as purchasing a transport service.
Digital storage must be a good because data occupy server hardware.
Bread is a want only because shops charge money for loaves.
Home maintenance is excluded from needs because homeowners already own the building.
tactical_explanations:
A luxury handbag is status and style spending, not a basic household need like food or shelter.

So the statement is True.

The ticket buys the right to be carried — transport as a service — even though a paper or digital ticket is the receipt.

So the statement is True.

Customers usually buy storage capacity as a service from a provider. Server hardware belonging to the host does not turn the customer’s rented storage into a tangible good they own.

So the statement is False.

Bread remains a staple food need whether or not shops charge for it. Price is the exchange mechanism, not what demotes bread into a mere want.

So the statement is False.

Owning the building does not remove the need to keep it safe and usable; maintenance supports continued shelter.

So the statement is False.

title: Winter Market Vendors
context: Consider a winter market where a woodworker sells chairs and a musician performs for tips beside the same stall row. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Visitors buying chairs or dropping tips participate in exchange as households or individuals.
Choosing hot drinks from a vendor satisfies a want for warmth more than a strict survival need in mild weather.
Craft sellers are households only because they stand in cold weather.
Artisans never economise because they can always carve more wood overnight.
Tips prove the music is a good because coins are tangible.
tactical_explanations:
Paying for a chair or tipping the musician is exchange: visitors hand over money for goods or a performance.

So the statement is True.

In mild weather a hot drink is comfort more than survival heating. That places it nearer a want for warmth than a strict survival need.

So the statement is True.

Standing in the cold does not define the role. Craft sellers organise production and sale of chairs — entrepreneurial activity — regardless of outdoor temperature.

So the statement is False.

Wood, tools, and overnight hours are limited. “Carve more later” still competes with sleep and other orders; artisans economise materials and time.

So the statement is False.

Coins pay for a performance service. Tangible tips do not convert the music itself into a good.

So the statement is False.

title: Universal Economic Participation
context: Analyze claims that nobody can fully escape economic life and decision-making. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Volunteering at a shelter uses scarce hours that could have been sold as paid labour elsewhere.
Governments delaying an infrastructure project still decide how to allocate the unchanged budget elsewhere.
Businesses closing for a holiday still decide how to allocate limited staff availability before and after the break.
Even unpaid household chores allocate scarce time among cooking, cleaning, and childcare.
Students choosing between sleep and revision allocate a scarce resource called time.
tactical_explanations:
Shelter hours could have been sold as paid work. Using them unpaid still spends scarce time — an economic allocation even without a wage.

So the statement is True.

Delaying one project frees the same budget line for other uses. The postponement is an allocation decision, not an escape from scarcity.

So the statement is True.

A holiday closure still requires rostering scarce staff before and after the break. Timing the shutdown is itself an economic choice about limited availability.

So the statement is True.

Unpaid chores still burn limited hours among cooking, cleaning, and childcare.

So the statement is True.

Sleep and revision cannot both fill the same night hour. Students allocate scarce time between rest and study whether or not money is involved.

So the statement is True.

title: Exchange and Need Fulfilment
context: Review how exchange connects needs and wants to goods and services in markets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Needs and wants on both sides motivate exchange because each party values what it receives.
Businesses exchange with suppliers to obtain inputs needed for their own production processes.
Exchange can occur internationally when an Austrian retailer imports textiles from a foreign producer.
Buying festival merchandise satisfies a want through exchange with an event entrepreneur.
Medicine sales are gifts because health is essential.
tactical_explanations:
Each party enters exchange because it values the incoming good or service more than what it gives up — needs and wants on both sides.

So the statement is True.

Buying inputs from suppliers is firm-to-firm exchange aimed at the buyer’s own production needs, not only at final consumers.

So the statement is True.

An Austrian retailer importing textiles is cross-border exchange with a foreign producer.

So the statement is True.

Festival merchandise is a want fulfilled by paying an event seller — household or visitor exchanging with an entrepreneur.

So the statement is True.

Essential medicines are still usually sold for payment. Calling a pharmacy sale a “gift” because health matters confuses the importance of the need with the form of the transfer. Paid medicine is exchange, not a present.

So the statement is False.

title: Economising in Service Businesses
context: Analyze economising behaviour in firms that chiefly supply services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A law firm allocates limited partner hours among client cases during a busy quarter.
Service entrepreneurs need no customers because advice is intangible.
Service firms face no scarcity because services are intangible.
Service purchases remove economising because labour is performed by others.
Fuel costs do not matter for service firms because customers pay fees.
tactical_explanations:
Partner hours in a busy quarter are limited; the firm ranks which client matters get those hours.

So the statement is True.

Advice has value only if someone wants it. Without customers, the intangible service earns nothing and the practice cannot cover costs.

So the statement is False.

Intangibility does not invent infinite lawyer hours or infinite server capacity. Service firms still face scarce skilled labour, diary slots, and support staff.

So the statement is False.

Hiring others to perform labour shifts who works; the buyer still economises fees, and the firm still economises its own payroll. Outsourcing does not delete scarcity.

So the statement is False.

Many service firms run vehicles or heat premises; fuel and energy still hit costs even when revenue comes as fees.

So the statement is False.

title: Foundations of Economic Life
context: Assess integrated claims about households, entrepreneurs, scarcity, and exchange. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The economy involves households and entrepreneurs exchanging goods and services to address needs and wants.
Goods are tangible items; services are intangible activities performed for someone.
Scarcity requires economising by all actors with limited resources.
Only wholesale trade among firms counts as exchange.
Only people who open businesses make economic decisions.
tactical_explanations:
Households and entrepreneurs meet in markets: goods and services move to address needs and wants. That interaction is the core picture of economic life in this chapter.

So the statement is True.

Goods have tangible form; services are intangible activities performed for someone — the standard split.

So the statement is True.

Limited resources force every actor — household, firm, or government — to economise rather than satisfy every claim at once.

So the statement is True.

Retail checkouts, second-hand sales between neighbours, and barter among classmates are exchange too. Wholesale deals among firms are only one channel — not the whole of exchange.

So the statement is False.

Consumers, students, and retirees make scarce-resource decisions constantly. Opening a business is not required to participate in economic life.

So the statement is False.

title: Elif: tutoring or unpaid internship
context: Consider elif can keep tutoring for 400 euros monthly or take an overlapping unpaid architecture internship. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Accepting the internship means opportunity cost is 400 euros monthly tutoring income forgone.
Because the internship pays nothing, choosing it has no opportunity cost at all.
Keeping tutoring means giving up career experience and prospects from the internship.
Opportunity cost must always be expressed only in euros with no other dimensions allowed.
Elif still allocates scarce time between tutoring and internship despite being a student.
tactical_explanations:
Accepting the unpaid internship uses the same hours Elif now spends tutoring. Those hours currently bring in 400 euros a month, so that forgone tutoring income is the opportunity cost of the internship.

So the statement is True.

Zero pay on the internship does not erase opportunity cost. The scarce input is Elif’s time; once she commits Saturday (or weekday) hours to architecture work, she cannot earn the 400 euros from tutoring with those same hours.

So the statement is False.

If she keeps tutoring, she forgoes the unpaid internship’s career signal — studio experience, portfolio pieces, and contacts that could help later applications. That forgone experience is an opportunity cost even though it is not a wage.

So the statement is True.

Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone. Value can be money, experience, leisure, or future prospects. Nothing in the definition locks the measure to euros alone.

So the statement is False.

Elif is still choosing how to spend limited hours. Students face the same scarce-time problem as anyone else: tutoring and the internship compete for the same calendar slots.

So the statement is True.

title: Simon: car wash or volunteering
context: Consider simon can earn 45 euros at a car wash or volunteer at an animal shelter on the same Saturday. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: If Simon volunteers, the opportunity cost is the 45 euros forgone from the car wash shift.
Scarcity concerns only money, so Simon faces no real scarcity when choosing how to use his Saturday.
Personal satisfaction from volunteering cancels any opportunity cost that might otherwise exist.
Because Simon is a teenager, scarce-resource allocation concepts do not apply to his Saturday.
The shelter's dog food cost is part of Simon's opportunity cost when he chooses volunteering.
tactical_explanations:
Volunteering at the shelter on Saturday means Simon cannot take the car-wash shift that pays 45 euros. That forgone pay is the opportunity cost of volunteering.

So the statement is True.

Scarcity is not only about cash. Simon has one Saturday; he cannot both wash cars and volunteer for the full day. Time is scarce here even if money were plentiful.

So the statement is False.

Enjoying volunteer work does not cancel opportunity cost. Satisfaction may make volunteering worthwhile, but the 45 euros from the car wash is still given up when he chooses the shelter.

So the statement is False.

Age does not exempt anyone from scarcity. A teenager’s Saturday hours are still limited; allocating them between paid work and volunteering is exactly the scarce-resource problem.

So the statement is False.

The shelter’s dog-food bill is the organisation’s cost, not Simon’s opportunity cost. His opportunity cost is what *he* forgoes — chiefly the 45-euro car-wash earnings — by volunteering.

So the statement is False.

title: Three actors, one week
